title: Ecommerce Catalogue Shoot vs Fashion Lookbook: Studio Setup Guide

children.text: An ecommerce catalogue shoot and a fashion lookbook need almost opposite studio setups. Here's how to tell which one you're actually booking for.

layout.content: Ecommerce Catalogue Shoot vs Fashion Lookbook: Studio Setup Guide

Brands planning their next shoot often book the wrong kind of studio because an ecommerce catalogue shoot and a fashion lookbook sound like the same thing but need almost opposite setups. A catalogue shoot is built for speed and consistency across dozens or hundreds of SKUs; a lookbook is built for mood, styling, and a handful of hero images that carry a brand's story. Booking a space suited to one when you actually need the other means paying for equipment you won't use, or missing equipment you can't shoot without. This guide breaks down what each shoot type actually needs from a studio, how the setups differ on backdrop, lighting, and crew, what both cost in Delhi NCR, and how to decide which one your next shoot calls for.
What a Catalogue Shoot Is Built For

A catalogue shoot exists to make every product look the same way, shot after shot, so a buyer scrolling a listing page sees consistency rather than variation. The job isn't to make any single image beautiful; it's to make every image in a 50, 100, or 300-SKU batch match. That means a plain, usually white or light grey, seamless backdrop that never moves between products, a fixed lighting setup that doesn't need re-balancing for each item, and a camera position locked to the same angle and distance so crops line up across the whole range. Marketplaces like Amazon, Flipkart, and Meesho also enforce strict background and framing rules for the primary listing image, so the studio setup is partly dictated by compliance, not just aesthetics.
What a Lookbook Shoot Needs Instead

A lookbook shoot exists to tell a story about a collection, not to standardise it. The brief usually asks for mood, movement, and a sense of who the brand is, which means the backdrop, lighting, and even the location can change from look to look. Where a catalogue shoot locks the lighting rig in place, a lookbook shoot adjusts it constantly: softer light for one look, harder contrast for another, a coloured gel or a textured backdrop for a hero frame. The studio needs enough floor space for full-body and movement shots, a real changing area with a rail and mirror, and room for hair and makeup touch-ups between looks, none of which a pure product studio is built to provide.
Studio Setup Comparison: Backdrop, Lighting, and Space
Side by side, the two shoot types pull a studio in opposite directions on nearly every setup decision.

items: Backdrop: catalogue shoots need one fixed, seamless, neutral sweep that never changes; lookbooks often need two or three options, including textured or coloured backdrops for hero looks
Lighting: catalogue shoots want a repeatable, evenly balanced setup that stays identical for every SKU; lookbooks want an adjustable rig that can shift mood frame to frame
Floor space: catalogue shoots can work in a compact setup since products don't move much; lookbooks need enough room for full-body frames, movement, and sometimes two models at once
Changing and prep area: largely irrelevant for a catalogue shoot; essential for a lookbook, where outfit changes happen every 10-20 minutes
Tethering and review: both benefit from a tether station, but it matters more for catalogue work, where a team is checking consistency across a large batch in real time

layout.content: A studio built to shoot 200 identical-background product shots and a studio built to shoot 20 styled fashion looks are solving different problems, even when they're the same four walls with different gear swapped in.
Crew and Workflow Differences

The team on set looks different too. A catalogue shoot typically runs with a photographer and someone prepping and handing off products in sequence: steaming, cleaning, and sorting by shot type so the camera setup barely changes between items. A lookbook shoot needs a stylist managing the rail and the changeovers, hair and makeup for touch-ups between looks, and usually one or two models, on top of the photographer. The pacing is different as well: a catalogue shoot moves through items in seconds once lighting is dialled in, while a lookbook shoot budgets 10-20 minutes per outfit change for styling, fitting, and touch-ups before the camera even comes back up. Trying to run both workflows through the same booked hours, say shooting white-background product shots and styled lifestyle looks back to back, is one of the most common reasons either type of shoot runs over its booked time.
What Each Shoot Costs in Delhi NCR

Studio rates reflect the setup difference directly. A basic, equipped studio suited to catalogue work, with a seamless white backdrop and fixed lighting, typically runs ₹1,000-2,500 per hour in Delhi NCR, with half-day packages for a large SKU batch landing around ₹8,000-16,000. A studio set up for fashion lookbooks, with adjustable lighting and a proper changing area, generally runs ₹1,500-4,000 per hour, and a full day covering 15-20 looks with a photographer, styling, and basic hair and makeup commonly lands in the ₹25,000-60,000 range once everyone on the crew is factored in. The gap isn't really the studio floor space; it's that a lookbook day bundles far more people and more setup changes into the same booking.
Choosing the Right Studio for Your Shoot

Before booking, settle what the images are actually for. If the output is going straight to a marketplace listing or a product grid on your own site, you need catalogue consistency, not mood, and a compact white-background studio will outperform a fashion-oriented space on both speed and cost. If the output is a seasonal lookbook, a press kit, or brand storytelling content, consistency matters far less than styling, movement, and a studio that can actually change its setup between looks without losing the day to re-rigging. Many brands running both end up booking two different kinds of sessions rather than trying to force one studio and one crew to do both jobs well.
FAQs: Catalogue Shoots vs Lookbook Shoots
Can one studio handle both a catalogue shoot and a lookbook shoot?

Some larger studios offer both a fixed product set and a separate area with changing space and adjustable lighting, which works if you're booking them as distinct sessions. Trying to shoot both in the same continuous block usually costs more time than it saves, since the crew has to re-rig lighting and backdrop between the two shot types.
Do I need a stylist for a catalogue shoot?

Usually not in the way a lookbook needs one. Catalogue shoots benefit more from someone prepping and handing off products (steaming, cleaning, sorting by shot type) than from a stylist managing wardrobe changes, since there's no model or outfit changeover to manage.
How many looks or SKUs fit in a single studio day?

A catalogue shoot with simple white-background shots can realistically cover 100-150+ SKUs in a half day once lighting is dialled in. A lookbook shoot with one model typically covers 10-30 looks in a full day, depending on styling complexity and how many angles each look needs.
Is a lookbook shoot always more expensive than a catalogue shoot?

Per hour of studio time, not necessarily; lookbook studios often charge only slightly more than catalogue studios. The bigger cost difference comes from the crew: a lookbook day usually adds a stylist, hair and makeup, and model fees on top of the studio and photographer, while a catalogue shoot's main added cost is usually just the photographer's per-SKU or per-hour rate.
Which shoot type should a new D2C brand book first?

Most new D2C brands need marketplace-ready catalogue images before they need a lookbook, since listings can't go live without compliant product photos. A lookbook is usually the next investment, once there's a catalogue to build a brand story around.

Final Takeaways
A catalogue shoot and a fashion lookbook ask a studio for almost opposite things, so the right booking starts with knowing which one you're actually running before you ever look at a studio listing.
